extracted.intended_audience: scientists, students, and readers interested in the foundations and philosophy of physical science
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and evaluating competing definitions and conceptual uses of 'matter' in physical science, with emphasis on the perceptual/conceptual distinction and principles of scientific method. The text offers canons and illustrative examples (e.g., waves, atoms) to judge which usages are scientifically legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon: Do not ascribe phenomenal existence to concepts without perceptual equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: To no concept, however invaluable it may be as a means of describing the routine of perceptions, ought phenomenal existence to be ascribed until its perceptual equivalent has been actually disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fundamental canon of scientific method warns against projecting conceptual constructs (molecules, atoms, geometrical ideals) into the realm of perceptual reality unless there is corresponding perceptual evidence. Violating it leads to antinomies and metaphysical assertions. Example: treating atoms/ideal surfaces as perceptual realities forces contradictions about volume and surface flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Matter is 'that which moves'
rubrics_metrics.description: Some writers define matter as the thing which moves in the phenomenal world; i.e., matter is that which moves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text critiques this as circular and inadequate for scientific definition: motion, in perception, is change of sense-impressions, and defining matter as 'that which moves' simply names the moving thing without describing or making it intelligible. The author suggests restating the question in conceptual terms (what conceptual types of motion best describe perceptual stages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Matter as a primary conception of the human mind
rubrics_metrics.description: "Matter is a primary conception of the human mind" — a definition offered in some elementary textbooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation is judged obscure and paralogistic. If taken to mean we can intuitively form a conception of what moves, it may indicate correspondence between perceptual and conceptual spheres; but it fails to give a clear, definite idea of 'matter' (unlike a clear conception such as a circle). The text treats such metaphysical-sounding statements skeptically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Matter via energy transfer (Clerk-Maxwell)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Matter is that which may have energy communicated to it from other matter, and which may in its turn communicate energy to other matter," with energy in turn defined as "that which ... is continually passing from one portion of matter to another."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author points out the circularity (matter defined via energy and energy via matter). Such definitions may express conceptual processes useful for description but do not advance understanding of what matter is; they merely restate that matter is that which moves/transfers energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Matter as perceptible or as that acted on/by force (Thomson & Tait)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Matter ... as that which can be perceived by the senses, or as that which can be acted upon by, or can exert, force."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage examines whether 'force' here is a direct object of sense (muscular sense) and argues that if a physical definition is not psychologically true it cannot be physically true. It questions whether senses would classify colour, hardness, pain as matter and stresses the need to relate physical definitions to psychological/sensory experience to avoid metaphysical postulation of 'things-in-themselves.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Matter as that which occupies space
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Tait's working definition: "Matter is whatever can occupy space."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text analyzes whether this refers to perceptual or conceptual space. If conceptual, matter becomes a geometrical form; if perceptual, only groups of sense-impressions can 'occupy' space. The author concludes that this definition tends to identify matter with relatively permanent groups of sense-impressions (a useful classification), but it does not justify postulating an unknowable substratum beyond perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: Scientific classifications should group sense-impressions, not postulate unknowable substrata
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifying certain more-or-less permanent groups of sense-impressions as 'material' is scientifically useful, but this classification throws no light on matter as an unknowable cause of sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recommended scientific stance is operational/classificatory: treat 'material groups' as stable patterns of perceptions (cf. J.S. Mill's 'permanent possibility of sensation') instead of asserting metaphysical 'things-in-themselves.' This avoids metaphysical fetishes in science while preserving useful descriptive concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: Physical definitions must accord with psychological (perceptual) truth
rubrics_metrics.description: If a physical definition is not psychologically true, it is not physically true; science and psychology must be in mutual relationship and intercommunication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must probe and question every statement and check physical claims against psychological experience (contents of perception are sense-impressions and stored sense-impresses). Example: calling force a 'direct object of sense' must be examined from the standpoint of whether force is actually a sense-impression or a metaphysical moving agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic: Impenetrability is relative, not an absolute test of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Common-sense attributes matter with impenetrability (and hardness), but impenetrability can only be relative: one thing is impenetrable relative to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: light penetrates glass though birds cannot; electric oscillations penetrate brick though light may not. The concept of impenetrability fails as an absolute defining property of matter. Considering atoms and whether they are penetrable remains unsettled; hypotheses of impenetrability may help explain phenomena but are not logically necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic: Hardness (muscular sense-impression) is not characteristic of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardness is a muscular sense-impression frequently associated with material groups, but it cannot be the essential test of matter's existence or nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardness (and softness or heaviness) are sense-impressions describable in terms of relative accelerations; many things termed matter are not hard, and some material entities produce no hardness impression. Thus hardness is not a necessary or sufficient characteristic to define matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: Individuality of a perceptual group does not imply sameness of underlying substratum
rubrics_metrics.description: Sameness or permanence of a phenomenal group of sense-impressions does not necessarily indicate a permanent identical substratum underlying it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative example: a wave on the sea appears as the same 'thing' though its substratum (the water molecules) changes continuously; waves can combine and separate preserving individual 'characteristics' despite changing substrata. By analogy, atoms could be penetrable or have varying substrata while still accounting for reproducible phenomena. Therefore permanence of perceptual phenomena need not imply an unchanging imperceptible entity.
